questions.stem: An 80-year-old woman presented with a nonhealing ulcerative lesion on her left earlobe. She was from central Texas and spent many hours a day working on her ranch. The lesion had not responded to empiric cephalexin. A biopsy of the lesion was performed. Histology: histiocytes in the dermis are filled with small round structures that have both a nucleus and kinetoplast.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely organism?
questions.explanation: Leishmania mexicana This is a case of cutaneous leishmaniasis acquired from the bite of an infected sandfly. The amastigotes of Leishmania will be seen in histiocytes while those of Trypanosoma cruzi will be seen in somatic cells (i.e., cardiac myocytes). Histoplasma can be seen in histiocytes as a small budding yeast but will not have a kinetoplast. Candida also does not have a kinetoplast and will show budding forms and possibly pseudohyphae depending on the species. Acanthamoeba is a free-living ameba that will have cysts and trophozoites when seen in tissues.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q36

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy returns from a trip to Argentina. He spent time hiking and on the beach and received numerous insect bites. A few weeks after he returned, he developed a gradually enlarging ulcer on his leg. The lesion began as a papule that then ulcerated. He has not had fevers or significant drainage from the ulceration. On examination, he had a 3 cm ulcer with an erythematous base and a raised border. There was no purulent drainage or surrounding cellulitis. Evaluations for bacterial and mycobacterial infections are unrevealing, and a parasitic infection is suspected.
questions.lead_in: Which of the following agents would be expected to have activity against the most likely causative pathogen?
questions.explanation: Paromomycin This patient likely has cutaneous leishmaniasis. Therapeutic options include observation, local treatment with cryotherapy or paromomycin, and systemic therapy with azoles, miltefosine, amphotericin, pentavalent antimonials, or pentamidine.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q48

questions.stem: A 33-year-old Somalian man presented with a 6-month history of fever, weight loss, abdominal discomfort, and swelling. He had also noticed recurrent epistaxis. He had left Somalia 1 year before his symptoms began. On examination, he was cachectic, with bipedal edema. His spleen was palpable 8 cm below the left costal margin. There were lymph nodes palpable in both inguinal chains. Investigations: Hemoglobin 85 g/L (130–180) Platelets 68 ×109/L (150–400) White cell count 1.8 ×109/L (4.0–11.0) Albumin 24 g/L (37–49) HIV Ag/Ab negative Bone marrow aspirate (see image):
questions.lead_in: What is the treatment of choice?
questions.explanation: Liposomal amphotericin B Liposomal amphotericin B is rapidly effective against visceral leishmaniasis and relatively nontoxic. It is the drug of choice for ill patients with visceral leishmaniasis as it is the best tolerated, and patients show a rapid response (afebrile within 1 week, and normalization of clinical signs and laboratory abnormalities within 2 weeks). (Image from Assessments. In Cohen J, Powderly W , Opal S, eds. Infectious Diseases. 4th ed. Elsevier; 2017.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q40

questions.stem: An 18-year-old woman presented with skin lesions on her right forearm and right cheek. They had developed gradually, from small papules which had enlarged and become nodular. She had emigrated from Afghanistan 4 months previously. She had no other known medical problems and was not taking any regular medications. A skin biopsy was taken.
questions.lead_in: What parasitic stage is most likely to be found in the biopsy?
questions.explanation: Amastigotes In cutaneous leishmaniasis, amastigotes multiply in dermal macrophages near the site of inoculation. (Image from Assessments. In Cohen J, Powderly W , Opal S, eds. Infectious Diseases. 4th ed. Elsevier; 2017.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q40

cohort_answer.text: Histopath (tissue)/bone marrow – amastigotes; Culture – promastigotes; Blood Smear/microscopy – promastigotes. || AmB; Pentavalent antimonial e.g. Sodium stibogluconate; Miltefosine.

questions.question: 17. Someone went in rural India for several months. He took mefloquine for malaria prophylaxis regularly and also took once or twice cipro. He seeks medical advice because of weight loss, fever and abdominal discomfort. Blood work reveals pancytopenia, hypoalbuminemia and hypergammaglobulinemia.

parts.text: What is the most probable diagnosis?
b) Name the single most likely pathogen (genus and species)
c) What specimens and which tests would you perform to confirm diagnosis?
d) Name 2 drugs that could be used to treat this patient

cohort_answer.text: Diagnosis: Visceral Leishmaniasis (Kala-azar). Pathogen: Leishmania donovani. Specimens/tests: Splenic or bone marrow aspirate for microscopy, PCR and culture; Serum for serology & PCR; PCR from tissue. Drugs: Liposomal amphotericin B; Pentavalent antimony (Sodium stibogluconate, meglumine antimoniate); Miltefosine; Fluconazole.

questions.question: A woman returns from the Brazilian Amazon with an ulcerating skin lesion. A picture is shown.

parts.text: What is the diagnosis?
Name 4 characteristics that would indicate complex disease requiring systemic treatment.
Name 2 drugs from different classes currently recommended for therapy.

questions.model_answer:
a) Diagnosis: cutaneous leishmaniasis (New World, likely Leishmania [Viannia] species given Brazilian Amazon exposure).
b) Four features of complex disease requiring systemic treatment: (1) Species associated with mucosal leishmaniasis (Viannia subgenus from the mucosal belt of Bolivia/Brazil/Peru). (2) More than 4 lesions of significant size, or an individual lesion ≥5 cm. (3) Lesion location unsuitable for local therapy (face, ears, eyelids, lips, fingers, toes, genitalia) or large regional adenopathy/subcutaneous nodules. (4) Immunosuppressed host, or unusual patterns such as leishmaniasis recidivans, diffuse, or disseminated cutaneous leishmaniasis.
c) Two drugs from different classes: pentavalent antimony (e.g., sodium stibogluconate or meglumine antimoniate) and miltefosine (or liposomal amphotericin B as an alternative parenteral option).

questions.question: 9. A patient returns from Brazil with fever, pancytopenia, HSM, weight loss. Workup is negative for bacterial and viral etiologies and so you suspect visceral leishmaniasis

parts.text: What are 4 diagnostic modalities that can be used to confirm VL (modalities was the word used, not samples)
What is the treatment of choice for VL in North America?
What are 2 other drugs from different classes that could be used?

cohort_answer.text: Diagnostic modalities: NAAT, Culture + isoenzyme analysis, Serology (most useful for VL), Histopathology (amastigotes). Treatment of choice: Liposomal AmB. Other drugs: Miltefosine, Sodium stibogluconate

questions.model_answer: Four diagnostic modalities for visceral leishmaniasis: (1) Bone marrow aspirate with Giemsa stain for amastigotes (safer, preferred method in nonendemic settings like Canada). (2) Splenic aspiration (most sensitive parasitologic method, but carries hemorrhage risk and is not recommended in North America). (3) Serology (rK39 rapid immunochromatographic test or direct agglutination test). (4) PCR (blood, bone marrow, or tissue) for Leishmania DNA. First-line treatment in Canada: liposomal amphotericin B (drug of choice for visceral leishmaniasis outside East Africa). Two other treatments from different classes: pentavalent antimony (sodium stibogluconate/meglumine antimoniate) and miltefosine.

questions.question: PM 16. Person returns from Brazil with scabbed skin ulcer painless, not healing. (picture shown) [image-based question: painless scabbed skin ulcer]

parts.text: What are 4 clinical criteria used to consider this complex mandating therapy? (2)
2 intravenous treatment options from different classes (1 vs 2)

cohort_answer.text: Criteria: Size of lesion (>5cm); Number of lesions (>4 lesions >1cm); Location in cosmetically sensitive place (face, ears, eyelids, lips, genitalia); Mucosal involvement or strain at risk of mucocutaneous disease (Viannia spp. from 'Mucosal Belt' of Bolivia, Peru, Brazil); Immunocompromised (especially cell-mediated); Bulky regional lymphadenopathy. IV treatment: Liposomal Ampho B; Pentavalent antimonial (Sodium stibogluconate); pentamidine isethionate. (Oral options: Ketoconazole, Fluconazole, Miltefosine.)

questions.question: Q74 (2017 PM). Cutaneous leishmaniasis image. The patient was from some South American country. [image-based question: cutaneous leishmaniasis lesion]

parts.text: A) Asked what 4 clinical considerations would indicate tx?
B) Treatment?

cohort_answer.text: Considerations indicating treatment: Age and clinical progression (lesions worsening); Number >5 in different locations; Complexity (restricts joint mobility, prevents wearing clothes/shoes, nose/ear involvement); Size >5cm; Immunocompromised; Mucosal involvement; Exposed skin (especially facial); L. braziliensis isolated. Treatment: Liposomal AmB; Miltefosine PO (for all three types); Pentavalent antimony (for cutaneous only).

questions.question: [image-based question: picture of sporotrichoid spread with 4 different stains shown, asked to identify the organism for each]

parts.text: Stain 1 (Leischmania)
Stain of nocardia branching GPCs in chains
A gram stain with 30% GPC, rest looked either washed out or like GNC either solo or in short chains, clusters as well (Francisella tularensis)

cohort_answer.text: Stain 1: Leishmania. Stain 2: Nocardia (branching GPCs in chains). Stain 3: Francisella tularensis (gram stain with ~30% GPC, rest washed out/GNC solo or in short chains/clusters). Stain 4: Sporothrix (~2 microns in size).

questions.question: Q8 (2017 PM). Picture of cutaneous leishmaniasis. The patient was from some South American Country.

parts.text: What are 4 clinical considerations that would indicate treatment?
B) Treatment?

cohort_answer.text: Considerations: Immunocompromised status; Lesion >5cm; More than 4 lesions; Lesion over joint, face, fingers, toes, genitalia; Lesions caused by species known to cause mucocutaneous leish. Treatment: IV - Conventional amphotericin B deoxycholate, Lipid formulations of amphotericin B, Pentavalent antimonial (SbV) compounds, Pentamidine; Oral - Miltefosine (SAP), azole antifungals (ketoconazole, fluconazole); Topical - Thermal, Cryotherapy, Paromomycin.

questions.question: Q44 (2010 AM, 2009 AM, 2008). Patient from India who has "kala-azar"

parts.text: A) What is the name of the clinical syndrome and organism implicated?
B) 4 common clinical or lab manifestations?
C) Which tissue is most likely to yield a positive bx result?

cohort_answer.text: A) Clinical syndrome: visceral leishmaniasis. Organism: L. donovani or infantum. B) Clinical: high fever, hepatosplenomegaly, wasting/malnutrition, weight loss, edema, petechiae, weakness, abdominal fullness, pallor, LAD. Lab: pancytopenia, pronounced hypergammaglobulinemia, low albumin (high protein). C) Splenic aspirates - sensitivity 96-98%.

questions.question: Q44/Q45 (2010 AM, 2008). Patient from India who has "kala-azar". Picture of cutaneous leishmaniasis on hand.

parts.text: What is the thing on the picture?
C) Why is it important to determine the species?
D) Name 3 common agents used for treatment?

cohort_answer.text: L. viannia (brasiliensis), L. panamensis, L. guyanensis often seen in central/south America, can progress to mucosal leishmaniasis more frequently; patient should be screened for mucosal leish if acquired from these regions. Picture: Localized cutaneous leishmaniasis. Species determination important as some species associated with visceral/mucosal leishmaniasis impacting treatment decisions. Treatment agents: IV - Liposomal AmpB, pentavalent antimony, pentamidine; Topical - cryotherapy, 15% paromomycin, intra-lesional antimony; PO - miltefosine.
